{{Short description|Complex multiplication field}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''CM-field''' is a particular type of [[number field]], so named for a close connection to the theory of [[complex multiplication]]. Another name used is  '''J-field'''.

The abbreviation "CM" was introduced by [[Goro Shimura|Shimura]] and [[Yutaka Taniyama|Taniyama]].{{sfnp|Shimura|Taniyama|1961}}

==Formal definition==
A number field <math>K</math> is a CM-field if it is a [[quadratic extension]] <math>K/F</math> where the base field <math>F</math> is [[totally real field|totally real]] but <math>K</math> is [[totally imaginary field|totally imaginary]]; i.e., every embedding of <math>F</math> into <math>\C</math> lies entirely within <math>\R</math>, but  there is no embedding of <math>K</math> into <math>\R</math>.

In other words, there is a subfield <math>F</math> of <math>K</math> such that <math>K</math> is generated over <math>F</math> by a single square root of an element, say <math>\beta = \sqrt{\alpha}</math>, in such a way that the [[minimal polynomial (field theory)|minimal polynomial]] of <math>\beta</math> over the [[rational number field]] <math>\Q</math> has all its roots non-real [[complex number]]s. For this α should be chosen ''totally negative'', so that for each embedding σ of <math>F</math> into the real number field, <math>\sigma(\alpha) < 0</math>.

==Properties==
One feature of a CM-field is that [[complex conjugation]] on <math>\C</math> induces an automorphism on the field which is independent of its embedding into <math>\mathbb C</math>. In the notation given, it must negate <math>\beta</math>.

A number field <math>K</math> is a CM-field if and only if it has a "units defect", i.e. if it contains a proper subfield <math>F</math> whose unit group has the same <math>\mathbb Z</math>-rank as that of <math>K</math>.{{sfnp|Remak|1954}} In fact, <math>F</math> is the totally real subfield of <math>K</math> mentioned above. This follows from [[Dirichlet's unit theorem]].

==Examples==
* The simplest, and motivating, example of a CM-field is an [[imaginary quadratic field]], for which the totally real subfield is just the field of rationals.

* One of the most important examples of a CM-field is the [[cyclotomic field]] <math>\Q(\zeta_n)</math>, which is generated by a primitive <math>n</math>th [[root of unity]]. It is a totally imaginary [[quadratic extension]] of the [[totally real field]] <math>\Q(\zeta_n +\zeta_n^{-1})</math>. The latter is the fixed field of [[complex conjugation]], and <math>\Q(\zeta_n)</math> is obtained from it by adjoining a square root of <math> (\zeta_n+\zeta_n^{-1})^2-4 = (\zeta_n - \zeta_n^{-1})^2.</math>

* The union <math>\Q^\mathrm{CM}</math> of all CM fields is similar to a CM field except that it has infinite degree. It is a quadratic extension of the union of all totally real fields <math>\Q^\mathrm{R}</math>. The [[absolute Galois group]] <math>\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\Q}/\Q^\mathrm{R})</math> is generated (as a closed subgroup) by all elements of order 2 in <math>\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\Q}/\Q)</math>, and <math>\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\Q}/\Q^\mathrm{CM})</math> is a subgroup of index 2. The Galois group <math>\operatorname{Gal}(\Q^\mathrm{CM}/\Q)</math> has a [[Center (group theory)|center]] generated by an element of order 2 (complex conjugation) and the quotient by its center is the group <math>\operatorname{Gal}(\Q^\mathrm{R}/\Q)</math>.

* If <math>V</math> is a complex [[abelian variety]] of dimension <math>n</math>, then any abelian algebra <math>F</math> of endomorphisms of <math>V</math> has rank at most <math>2n</math> over <math>\Z</math>. If it has rank <math>2n</math> and <math>V</math> is simple then <math>F</math> is an order in a CM-field. Conversely any CM field arises like this from some simple complex abelian variety, unique up to [[isogeny]].

*One example of a totally imaginary field which is not CM is the number field defined by the polynomial <math>x^4 + x^3 - x^2 - x + 1</math>.
